1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: Basic information: Male patient, 55 years old, was admitted to the Department of Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine (main campus) inpatient ward of our hospital on Day +12, with the chief complaints of "precordial pain for 13 days, hypoxemia with fever for 11 days, and multiple-site bleeding for 5 days." The patient is a 55-year-old retired military physician with a history of hypertension. He developed an acute Stanford type A aortic dissection while fishing and was transferred to a local hospital the next day for total arch replacement and aortic valve replacement. Postoperatively, he subsequently developed right pneumothorax, VAP, and secondary septic shock in the ICU. He was supported with VA ECMO locally, but infection control was poor, and he developed oxygenator thrombosis, bleeding at multiple sites, and renal insufficiency, requiring combined CRRT. Thirteen days before admission (12-8), he developed precordial pain without an obvious precipitating factor, described as tearing pain to the left of the area above the xiphoid process, accompanied by near-syncope and chest tightness. He presented to a local hospital and was diagnosed with aortic dissecting aneurysm (type A). He then underwent emergency total aortic arch replacement (mechanical aortic valve replacement, Sun procedure) at a local tertiary hospital on 12-9 and was transferred to the ICU postoperatively for treatment. Eleven days before admission, he had sudden decreased oxygen saturation (details of blood gas not available). Chest X-ray showed right pneumothorax with 90% compression, and right closed thoracic drainage was performed. Repeat chest X-ray showed good lung re-expansion. Ten days before admission (12-11), oxygenation continued to worsen. Blood gas (support conditions unknown) showed pH 7.37, PaCO2 38 mmHg, and PaO2 75 mmHg, accompanied by fever with temperature 38.4℃. CBC showed elevated leukocyte count, elevated infection and inflammatory markers, and elevated transaminases and creatinine. Chest X-ray showed extensive exudation and right lung consolidation. Meropenem 1 g q12h was given for anti-infective treatment, along with sivelestat sodium 0.4 g QD and ulinastatin 100,000 U q8h; other treatments included expectorant therapy, hepatoprotective therapy, and diuresis. Nine days before admission (12-12) at 1 pm, left femoral V-A ECMO was initiated because oxygenation could not be maintained and was complicated by toxic-infectious shock. Bivalirudin was used for anticoagulation, with an APTT target of around 50 s, and vancomycin was added for anti-infective treatment. Eight days before admission, CBC showed WBC 14.36*10^9/L, neutrophils 93.8%, and PCT 40.5 ng/ml. Worsening infection was considered. Sputum culture and send-out blood NGS showed Acinetobacter baumannii (specific susceptibility unknown). Six days before admission, antibiotics were adjusted to meropenem 1 g q12h combined with tigecycline (Tygacil) 50 mg q12h; on 12-18, tigecycline was adjusted to 100 mg q12h. Five days before admission, the pericardial/mediastinal drainage changed from light yellow to bloody drainage, accompanied by epistaxis and oozing from puncture sites. Bivalirudin was stopped, and hemostatic treatment with tranexamic acid, fibrinogen, coagulation factors, and vitamin K led to improvement. Subsequent repeat chest X-ray showed worsening pulmonary exudation compared with before. WBC and PCT were markedly increased. Renal insufficiency with hypernatremia developed, and CRRT was performed once (discontinued due to ECMO alarm, 12 h). One day before admission, repeat chest X-ray showed pulmonary exudation had significantly worsened compared with before (Figure 1). Given the critical condition, he was transferred to our department for treatment. The patient has had hypertension for more than 10 years, with a highest recorded blood pressure of 160/120 mmHg. He is currently taking antihypertensive medications: "sacubitril/valsartan 1 tablet once daily, metoprolol 1 tablet once daily, irbesartan 1 tablet once daily"; blood pressure control is unknown. He was diagnosed with chronic viral hepatitis B, inactive HBsAg carrier state, 10 years ago. He has a 30-year smoking history, averaging 20 cigarettes/day, and quit smoking 5 years ago. Family history is unremarkable. Considering the prolonged ECMO run time and associated coagulation dysfunction, oxygenator thrombosis with consumptive coagulopathy was considered first. The plan was to replace the ECMO and then transport him by fixed-wing aircraft to reduce the risk during transport of increased oxygenator thrombosis and unstable oxygenation and blood pressure. Considering the long transport time and involvement of multiple means of transportation, our hospital's Cardiohelp device was taken for outside transport to reduce risks such as circuit kinking. Therefore, Dr. Wang Rui from our hospital's respiratory ICU went to the local hospital to replace the oxygenator and transport the patient. Day +11, 16:00-19:50, transfer flight Beijing to Urumqi; Day +11, 20:30-21:20, ECMO replacement and departure; Day +11, 23:00-Day +12, 2:00, Urumqi to Beijing. After landing at Beijing Capital Airport, he was transferred by 120 ambulance to our hospital's RICU, arriving at 2:45 on Day +12. Physical examination after admission: T 37.9℃, P 82 beats/min, R 27 breaths/min, BP 115/63 mmHg (continuous norepinephrine infusion). He was sedated and receiving analgesia, RASS score -4. Breath sounds were coarse in both lungs, with abundant moist rales in both lower lungs, more prominent on the left. Heart rate 82 beats/min, regular rhythm, normal heart sounds, no murmur heard in the valvular auscultation areas. Abdomen soft, no mass palpated. No edema in either lower extremity. A longitudinal surgical incision was visible near the right inguinal ligament (backup incision for ECMO cannulation), with poor healing, a small amount of yellow secretion, and surrounding skin erythema. The following indwelling tubes/catheters were present on admission: ① endotracheal tube (Day 0) ② left femoral arteriovenous ECMO cannulas (Day +3) ③ left subclavian deep venous catheter (Day +3) ④ left closed thoracic drainage tube (Day 0) ⑤ right closed thoracic drainage tube (Day +11) ⑥ pericardial/mediastinal drainage tube (Day 0) ⑦ urinary catheter and gastric tube (Day 0). Repeat chest CT on admission (Figure 2): multiple areas of consolidation and patchy infiltrates in both lungs, most prominent in the left lower lung. Pericardial/mediastinal drainage and bilateral closed thoracic drainage tubes are in place. Status post surgery for aortic dissection; status post aortic valve replacement.

differential_diagnoses.name: Severe hospital-acquired pneumonia/ventilator-associated pneumonia (predominantly due to gram-negative bacilli, Acinetobacter baumannii infection highly suspected)
supporting_evidence: After postoperative transfer to the ICU, fever developed, with a body temperature of 38.4℃
CBC showed leukocytosis; 8 days earlier, WBC 14.36*10^9/L, neutrophils 93.8%, PCT 40.5 ng/ml

Chest radiograph showed diffuse infiltrates and right lung consolidation. Subsequent repeat examination indicated that the pulmonary infiltrates had worsened compared with previously, and the chest radiograph 1 day earlier showed markedly worsened infiltrates.
Repeat chest CT on admission showed multiple areas of consolidation and patchy infiltrative opacities in both lungs, more pronounced in the left lower lung.
Prolonged endotracheal intubation, ICU hospitalization, mechanical ventilation, and multiple invasive catheter placements are all high-risk factors for VAP
Sputum culture and send-out blood NGS showed Acinetobacter baumannii
On physical examination, numerous moist rales were heard in both lower lungs, more pronounced on the left.
opposing_evidence: The phase 1 information did not provide clear contradictory evidence.

differential_diagnoses.name: Infection-related acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)
supporting_evidence: Starting 10 days ago, oxygenation progressively worsened. Arterial blood gas showed PaO2 75 mmHg (support conditions unspecified), and subsequently V-A ECMO was initiated because oxygenation could not be maintained.
There is a clear background of severe infection/septic shock; the text mentions secondary septic shock and infectious toxic shock
Both chest radiograph and lung CT showed extensive bilateral pulmonary exudation, multiple consolidations, and patchy infiltrative opacities, which are imaging manifestations of diffuse lung injury.
Physical examination: respiratory rate 27 breaths/min, extensive moist rales in both lower lungs
Progressive worsening on imaging, suggesting an acute diffuse pulmonary parenchymal injury process
opposing_evidence: Stage 1 information did not provide data on lung compliance, oxygenation index, or exclusion of cardiogenic causes; ARDS cannot yet be established based on Stage 1 information alone.

differential_diagnoses.name: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema/postoperative heart failure-related pulmonary congestion
supporting_evidence: Recently underwent major cardiovascular surgery for type A aortic dissection, including total arch replacement and aortic valve replacement; postoperative hypoxemia and hemodynamic instability developed
Continuous norepinephrine infusion was required, indicating a need for circulatory support.
Prominent crackles in both lungs; imaging shows extensive bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, which may overlap with the appearance of pulmonary edema
Chest CT may show bilateral pleural effusions/pleural drainage tubes in place; postoperative volume overload and abnormal cardiac function are often accompanied by pleural effusion.
opposing_evidence: Accompanied by high fever and markedly elevated white blood cell count and PCT, this more strongly supports an infectious pulmonary lesion

Chest CT was described as showing multiple consolidations and patchy infiltrative opacities, more pronounced in the lower lungs, especially the left lower lobe, favoring infectious/inflammatory changes rather than simple cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
In phase 1, echocardiography, BNP, or clear evidence of left heart dysfunction was not provided

differential_diagnoses.name: Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage/hemorrhagic pulmonary lesion
supporting_evidence: Five days ago, bleeding developed at multiple sites, including pericardial and mediastinal drainage fluid becoming bloody, epistaxis, and oozing from puncture sites.
with a history of bivalirudin anticoagulation, prolonged ECMO run time, coagulation dysfunction, and coagulation factor consumption after membrane lung thrombosis
Pulmonary exudative opacities progressively worsen and may present as hemorrhagic infiltrates in the setting of severe coagulopathy
Progressive worsening of hypoxemia can be seen in alveolar hemorrhage
opposing_evidence: Hemoptysis or bloody airway secretions were not mentioned in the first stage
The concomitant presence of high fever, markedly elevated inflammatory markers, and microbiologic clues more strongly supports infectious pulmonary consolidation.
Imaging did not describe typical hemorrhagic manifestations predominantly characterized by diffuse ground-glass opacities

differential_diagnoses.name: Postoperative pleural infection/complicated pleural effusion or empyema
supporting_evidence: Postoperatively, bilateral closed thoracic drainage tubes were placed, suggesting a background of pleural space complications
CT and chest radiograph show bilateral pleural effusions and lower lung involvement, more severe in the left lower lung, consistent with pleural effusion with possible adjacent atelectasis/infection
Persistent fever, markedly elevated inflammatory markers, poor infection control
History of right pneumothorax treated with closed thoracic drainage; recently presented with bilateral chest drains in place, suggesting a complex pleural space problem
opposing_evidence: In the first stage, direct evidence such as pleural fluid characteristics, pleural fluid analysis, or pleural septations was not provided.
Multiple pulmonary consolidations and patchy infiltrates are more prominent, and the primary lesions may still be in the lung parenchyma.

stage2_input.text: Ancillary examinations 12-21: CBC: WBC: 23.2×10^9/L, NEU: 96.4%, HB: 84 g/L, PLT: 78×10^9/L. Blood chemistry: albumin 36.4 g/L, prealbumin 0.05 g/L, creatinine 299.6 umol/L, urea 74.24 mmol/L, sodium 162.8 mmol/L. NT-proBNP: 2694 pg/ml, cTNI 901.6 ng/ml. Blood gas (P-A/C, Pi 20 cmH2O, PEEP 6 cmH2O, FiO2 1.0, ECMO BF 2.65 L/min): lactate 1.7, P/F 78. Bronchoscopy: large amount of yellow sputum in the airway. Echocardiography: left ventricular hypertrophy, EF normal. After aggressive prone positioning and other postural drainage measures, the patient's oxygenation index and bilateral lung radiolucency improved significantly compared with admission, but PCT increased progressively. ECMO was considered a possible potential source of infection, and ECMO was removed on hospital day 3. The patient's PCT gradually decreased, but still fluctuated at a relatively high level (5-10 ng/ml). The right pleural drainage tube was removed on hospital day 7, and the left pleural drainage tube was removed on hospital day 13. On Day +27, the patient suddenly developed rupture and bleeding at the right femoral artery puncture site; after emergency vascular surgery, the wound healed well. After 1.5 months of adequate anti-infective treatment, the patient still had recurrent fever (Tmax 37.6-38℃), with low-level fluctuation of PCT (0.5-1.5 ng/ml). Repeat chest CT (2-02) showed: partial absorption of bilateral pulmonary inflammation compared with before; small left pleural effusion, decreased compared with before; exudative changes in the mediastinum, with mediastinal drainage tube in place; multiple small mediastinal lymph nodes visualized; full cardiac silhouette; postoperative changes of the aortic arch; high-density shadow at the aortic root, with no significant change from before; crescent-shaped low-density shadow in the wall of the ascending aorta, roughly similar to before (Figure 4). Echocardiography (2-03): status post aortic mechanical valve replacement + Sun's procedure; prosthetic mechanical valve at the aortic valve position with acceptable function; small regurgitation of the mechanical valve; patent flow in the artificial graft; left ventricular hypertrophy. After adequate anti-infective treatment, the patient's WBC and procalcitonin both decreased significantly compared with early after admission, and the indwelling chest drainage tubes and ECMO cannulas had all been removed. However, flocculent material was still draining from the pericardial/mediastinal drainage tube. The skin around the catheter insertion site was in good condition. The patient required ongoing CRRT, with deep venous catheter replacement every 7 days. Multiple repeat echocardiograms showed no valvular vegetation. The patient was conscious and able to cooperate with rehabilitation exercises.

recommended_exams.exam: Repeat thoracotomy to explore whether there is an infectious focus within the vascular graft
recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: On Day +57, after further MDT discussion, it was decided to perform a second thoracotomy to explore whether there were infectious lesions within the prosthetic vascular graft.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient is critically ill status post surgery for type A aortic dissection, total arch replacement, and mechanical aortic valve replacement. The early course was complicated by VAP, septic shock, ECMO support, CRRT, and multiple indwelling tubes/catheters. Although after 1.5 months of adequate anti-infective treatment the bilateral pulmonary inflammatory changes had partially resolved compared with before, the WBC count and PCT had decreased significantly compared with the early stage, repeated echocardiography showed no valvular vegetations, and the ECMO and pleural drainage tube had also been removed, the patient still had recurrent fever, and the pericardial/mediastinal drainage tube continued to drain flocculent material. Chest CT showed mediastinal exudative changes, a hyperdense shadow at the aortic root, and a crescentic low-density shadow in the wall of the ascending aorta, with little change compared with before, indicating that in addition to pulmonary infection and common catheter-related infection, infection at the surgical site, especially a prosthetic vascular graft-related infectious focus, must still be highly suspected. Prosthetic vascular graft infection is a serious postoperative complication and is difficult to completely exclude on the basis of routine imaging, laboratory tests, and ultrasound alone; once missed, it can lead to persistent uncontrolled infection and directly affect decisions regarding subsequent debridement, anti-infective therapy, and whether surgical intervention is needed. Because comprehensive MDT evaluation considered persistent occult mediastinal/surgical-site infection possible, the purpose of exploratory thoracotomy is to directly determine whether there is infection, fluid collection, purulent lesions, or poor drainage around the prosthetic vascular graft and within the lumen, thereby completing a key differential diagnosis; this would not only provide the most direct basis for confirming or excluding prosthetic vascular graft infection, but also provide decisive information for whether to proceed with mediastinal debridement, muscle flap transfer, and antibiotic adjustment.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Postoperative pathology: 1 piece of gray-white irregular tissue, diameter 0.6 cm. The specimen consists of degenerated necrotic tissue, inflammatory exudate, and blood clot.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient had long-term recurrent fever. Before surgery, there was persistent abnormal mediastinal drainage and imaging evidence of exudative mediastinal changes; however, after prolonged anti-infective treatment, the infection markers had improved significantly compared with those at admission. Clinically, it was necessary to further clarify the nature of the abnormal tissue and fluid collection observed during the second thoracotomy, and to distinguish among true prosthetic vascular graft-related infection, mediastinal abscess, and postoperative nonspecific inflammation, necrotic tissue, organized clot, or adhesion barrier membrane-related changes. Postoperative pathology can provide a histologic-level assessment of the intraoperative specimens and determine whether there is definite infectious pathology, whether necrosis and inflammatory exudate predominate, and whether the findings support mediastinal fibrous peel/organization changes, thereby compensating for the limitations of gross intraoperative inspection alone. This examination is critical for establishing the final etiology: if pathology does not support definite prosthetic vascular graft infection but instead suggests degenerative necrotic tissue, inflammatory exudate, and clot, this would better help exclude persistent bacterial prosthetic vascular graft infection, support postoperative local organization and lesions related to poor drainage, and on this basis guide the gradual discontinuation of antibiotics and a shift toward mediastinal debridement and repair; at the same time, it also reduces the risk of unnecessary prolonged intensive anti-infective treatment or more extensive surgical replacement.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: On Day +57, after repeat MDT discussion, it was decided to perform a second thoracotomy exploration to assess whether there was an infectious focus within the vascular graft. Intraoperatively, no definite infection was seen around the vascular graft; there was retrosternal effusion, considered to be due to poor drainage of the effusion caused by the retrosternal anti-adhesion membrane. Postoperative pathology: 1 piece of gray-white irregular tissue, diameter 0.6 cm; the specimen consisted of degenerative necrotic tissue, inflammatory exudate, and blood clot.

diagnostic_basis: Retrosternal fluid collection was seen during the second exploratory thoracotomy; poor drainage of the fluid was considered to be caused by the retrosternal anti-adhesion membrane.
Postoperative pathology: 1 piece of irregular gray-white tissue, 0.6 cm in diameter; the specimen consists of degenerative necrotic tissue, inflammatory exudate, and blood clot.
After mediastinal debridement + muscle flap transfer surgery, body temperature gradually returned to normal, and symptoms gradually improved

treatment_plan: Mediastinal debridement + muscle flap transfer surgery
treatment_response: The patient's body temperature gradually returned to normal after surgery
Pericardial and mediastinal drainage tubes were removed 2 weeks after surgery
After 4 months of rehabilitation in the RICU, he was discharged on Day +181.
At follow-up 1.5 years later, the patient had resumed normal life.
